newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan main ports to change wharfage charges.
newsitem.headline: Japan main ports to change wharfage charges.

text.p: Japan's eight big ports plan to change their wharfage system from May in an attempt to boost international competitiveness, shipping industry officials said on Thursday.

The planned change to the wharfage system at the ports of Kobe, Yokohama, Tokyo, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Osaka, Shimonoseki and Kita-Kyushu, will in effect lower fees for vessels docking for less than 12 hours, but raise charges for those berthing up to 24 hours, a Japanese Ship Owners' Association official said.
Currently, the ports charge 13.40 yen per gross registered ton (grt) for a set 24 hours.
The new system will charge 10.05 yen per grt for vessels docking up to 12 hours. An additional 6.75 yen will be added for every 12 hours thereafter.
Vessels such as containers and pure car carriers, which are increasingly used, are usually loaded or unloaded within 12 hours.
Other Japanese ports are expected to follow the move in rationalising the wharfage system.

Japanese port costs are well above international levels, and the shipping industry has seen business fleeing to neighbouring Asian countries where costs are roughly less than half the price of Japanese ports.
However, port authorities cite the need for costs other than wharfage to be lowered to lure business back.

"Wharfage accounts for only five to 10 percent of the total port charges, therefore we feel the need for other fees such as towage and stevedoring to come down," an official with the Port and Harbour Bureau of the city of Yokohama said.
The high costs of Japanese ports and the lack of transparency in the stevedore business have recently come under fire from the United States and European Union.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), is likely to come up with a decision on whether to impose sanctions on Japanese shipping firms for what Washington says are unfair practices at Japanese ports in the next three weeks.
The move follows steps taken last October by the European Union, calling for consultations with Japan under World Trade Organisation rules to make Japanese ports more accessible to foreign shippers.
